title: Modded NanoGPT Hits 29.90s LLM Pretraining World Record
summary: Developer achieves sub-30-second LLM pretraining world record on 8×H100 GPUs using modified NanoGPT framework. Full technical breakdown inside.
body_markdown:
**Officially launched on November 22, 2026.**


#### 💡 TL;DR


- Developer Amund achieved a 29.90-second LLM pretraining world record on 8×H100 GPUs using heavily modified NanoGPT code.
- The breakthrough leverages aggressive kernel fusion, mixed-precision optimization, and multi-node distributed training strategies to maximize GPU throughput.
- This milestone pushes the boundaries of training efficiency and demonstrates how targeted code optimizations can unlock extreme performance gains.


A developer has set a new world record for LLM pretraining speed, completing a full training run in just 29.90 seconds on a cluster of eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The achievement, documented by Amund on their technical blog, represents a breakthrough in training efficiency using a heavily modified version of Andrej Karpathy's NanoGPT framework. The sub-30-second milestone pushes the boundaries of what is possible with current hardware and aggressive software optimization.


## Record-Breaking Configuration and Methodology


The record run utilized eight H100 GPUs in a distributed training setup, with modifications spanning every layer of the training stack. Amund implemented custom kernel fusion to reduce memory bandwidth overhead, aggressive mixed-precision strategies to maximize throughput, and a carefully tuned data pipeline to eliminate I/O bottlenecks. The configuration trained a small-scale language model to convergence on a compact[pretraining corpus](https://emergent.sh/glossary/pretraining-corpus) , with validation loss curves confirming proper learning dynamics despite the extreme speed.


Unlike typical pretraining runs that span hours or days, this approach prioritizes end-to-end latency over model scale. The developer focused on minimizing every millisecond of overhead, from NCCL communication patterns to gradient accumulation strategies. Each optimization was benchmarked individually before integration, ensuring no regression in final model quality.


## Technical Optimizations Behind the Speed


The modified NanoGPT codebase incorporates several novel techniques. Kernel fusion reduces the number of GPU kernel launches by combining operations like layer normalization and attention computation into single CUDA kernels. Mixed-precision training uses FP8 for forward passes and FP16 for backward passes, with dynamic loss scaling to maintain numerical stability. The data loader was rewritten in C++ to prefetch batches three steps ahead, completely hiding disk I/O latency.


Distributed training coordination relied on a custom ring-allreduce implementation optimized for the H100's NVLink interconnect topology. Gradient synchronization overlaps with backward computation, and the optimizer step runs asynchronously on a dedicated CUDA stream. These changes collectively reduced per-step time from approximately 42 milliseconds in baseline NanoGPT to under 4 milliseconds in the final version.


## Release Date and Availability


The record attempt was officially completed on November 22, 2026, with full code and reproduction instructions published on Amund's technical blog. The modified NanoGPT implementation is available as open-source software, allowing researchers to validate the results and build upon the optimization techniques. Hardware requirements remain steep, requiring access to eight H100 GPUs with high-bandwidth interconnect, but the software stack can scale down to smaller configurations for experimentation.


## Implications for Training Efficiency Research


This milestone demonstrates that training speed is not purely a hardware problem. While H100 GPUs provide substantial raw compute, the gap between theoretical and achieved performance remains large in most codebases. By systematically eliminating overhead at every layer, developers can unlock performance gains that rival hardware upgrades. The techniques proven here, particularly around kernel fusion and asynchronous execution, are directly applicable to production training pipelines for larger models.


Future work may focus on extending these optimizations to multi-billion parameter models, where communication overhead and memory bandwidth become dominant bottlenecks. The sub-30-second barrier, once considered impossible for any meaningful training workload, now serves as a proof point for what is achievable with current-generation hardware and careful engineering.


## What This Means


The 29.90-second LLM pretraining record redefines expectations for training efficiency and highlights the untapped performance potential in existing hardware. For researchers and engineers, this work provides a roadmap for optimizing training pipelines beyond what frameworks offer out of the box. As models continue to scale, these techniques will become essential for managing costs and iteration speed. The achievement also underscores the value of open-source experimentation in pushing the limits of AI infrastructure.
